analysis.one_liner: Makes governments and their insurers pay damages when their officers violate constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2021 with 2 cosponsors, sent to House Judiciary subcommittees in November 2022, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a Reconstruction-era civil rights law so that victims of police misconduct can sue the federal government, states, and cities for money damages when a law enforcement officer violates their constitutional rights. It would override three Supreme Court-made shields: qualified immunity (protection for individual officers), sovereign immunity (protection of the federal and state governments from being sued), and the rule that cities are liable only when a violation flows from official policy or custom. Under the bill, liability would attach simply because the officer who caused the harm worked for the government, the same rule that applies to private employers.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by police — including victims of excessive force, false arrest, and unlawful searches — and their families. The bill's own findings point to departments that kept officers with records of misconduct, and the threat of lawsuits would push those departments to screen, train, and discipline officers better.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police misconduct and their families

how_it_helps.text: Creates an explicit federal right to sue the United States, states, and local governments for constitutional violations committed by their law enforcement officers, including through contractors [S2][S3].

Removes qualified immunity as a defense and ends the requirement that a victim prove a city's policy or custom caused the harm — liability attaches to the employer whenever its officer commits the violation [S2][S3].
Overrides state and federal sovereign immunity for these claims, meaning governments cannot hide behind immunity from being sued [S2][S3].

The bill's findings note that more than 18,000 police departments exist with no uniform training standard, and that as recently as 2017, 34 states did not require de-escalation training; employer liability is intended to create pressure to fix that [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local governments — and ultimately their taxpayers and liability insurers — would bear the cost of settlements and judgments in misconduct cases, and police departments would face the cost of stronger screening, training, and supervision of officers.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap damages or require insurance, so a wave of liability claims could strain municipal budgets, with costs falling on taxpayers in cities and states that can least afford them [S3].

Critics of ending qualified immunity argue that officers must make split-second life-or-death decisions and that open-ended liability would discourage people from joining or staying in policing; the bill's own findings acknowledge that officers face such split-second decisions [S3].

The bill shifts liability from individual officers to their government employers, so an officer's own wages are untouched — accountability would flow through department budgets and management rather than directly to the officer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims who today lose their cases at the summary-judgment stage because of qualified immunity or the Monell policy-or-custom requirement, this is the difference between no remedy and a real one. The cost side is real but manageable: governments already insure against much tort liability, and private employers face the same respondeat superior liability the bill would impose on governments. A well-designed version could pair open liability with state-administered insurance pools; as written, the bill sets the liability but leaves financing entirely to the states and cities.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee, was sent to two subcommittees in November 2022, and died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on December 20, 2021, with Reps. Hank Johnson and Jamie Raskin as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].

Nearly a year later, on November 1, 2022, it was referred to the subcommittees on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties and on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security; no hearing or markup followed [S5].
Only two members cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments, their insurers, and police departments are better off: no employer liability for officer misconduct was created, so qualified immunity, sovereign immunity, and the Monell policy-or-custom requirement all remain the law of the land.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and laid out findings that current law lets departments avoid liability for officer misconduct [S1][S3].

for.name: Reps. Hank Johnson and Jamie Raskin
for.role: Original cosponsors, House Judiciary Committee members

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (117th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the 13 months after it was referred, sending it to two subcommittees in the final months of the session [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the only two cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill received no Republican cosponsors; it also never advanced in a House where the Democratic majority's Judiciary Committee did not act on it [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: State and local governments (police departments and municipal treasuries)
industries.note: The bill would make governments financially responsible for constitutional violations by their officers, ending defenses (qualified immunity, sovereign immunity, the Monell policy-or-custom rule) that let them escape judgments. The bill died, so those shields remain intact.

Insurers already sell police-liability coverage and would absorb or reprice the new exposure; their interest in limiting payouts runs against broadening victims' access to damages. The bill's death leaves their market unchanged.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: While liability would rest with employers rather than individual officers, departments under financial pressure would hire, train, supervise, and discipline more strictly — exactly the incentive the bill's findings say is missing today [S3].
